title: Sakya Pandita
hookLine: the scholar of the Sakya school, well-known for his book of wise sayings

lines: A TIBETAN BOOK OF GOOD SENSE.
cards: Measure twice, cut once. Don't go to bed angry. Some families have a few lines like that, said by a grandmother so often that they stuck, and years later they come out of a grandchild's mouth at the oddest moments.
Tibet has a book of lines like that, short verses of good sense, small enough to learn by heart. The man who wrote it was a celebrated scholar, a master of logic and debate.
And he chose to put a lot of what he knew into sayings small enough to carry. Today, Sakya Pandita.

teach.h: A SCHOOL, AND A TITLE FOR A SCHOLAR.
teach.b: First, the name. Sakya is a school of Tibetan Buddhism, named for the monastery at its center.
Pandita is a Sanskrit title for a learned scholar; tradition says Tibetans gave him that title because he mastered the Indian sciences, from grammar to logic.
He also wrote a work on logic, the Treasury of Valid Reasoning. Second, the surprise.
This same scholar wrote the Treasury of Good Sayings, short verses about everyday life: how the wise and the foolish behave, how to treat friends, how to hold wealth, how to speak.
The verses lean on everyday pictures, from the house, the field and the road. Third, why a scholar would write this way. A long argument helps a student in the debating courtyard.

teach.h: A SAYING GOES HOME WITH YOU.
teach.b: A short saying goes home with the farmer and the trader, and comes back to mind when it's needed.

One saying credited to him runs roughly like this: even if you will die tomorrow, study today; you may not become wise in this life, but it is like saving wealth for the next. Fourth, his life outside the library.

teach.h: WORDS CARRIED TO A MONGOL COURT.
teach.b: Tradition says that late in life he traveled to the court of a Mongol prince, and that his teaching there helped shape how Mongol rulers and Tibetan teachers dealt with each other afterward.
The man who wrote about speaking well, the story goes, was asked to practice it in a foreign court, far from home.

how: In Tibetan communities, verses from Sakya Pandita's Treasury of Good Sayings are learned and quoted, and his work on logic is studied in monastic settings, especially in the Sakya school.

games.q: a friend says, "I'm too old to start learning this now. what's the point?" which answer is closest to the saying credited to Sakya Pandita?
o: "study today, even if you die tomorrow."
"only learn what pays off this year."
games.why: the saying credited to him says learning is never wasted: even if you don't become wise in this life, it is like saving wealth for the next.

practice: Choose one short saying: the one you just heard, about studying today even if you die tomorrow, or one from your own family or tradition.
Say it slowly on the out-breath, letting each word land, and when one word feels heaviest, stay with it for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Sakya Pandita. The great scholar of the Sakya school, master of logic, who wrote the Treasury of Good Sayings so wisdom could travel in small pieces. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit pandita: a learned one, a scholar. Tibetans gave him this title.

carryVoice: Your line: wise sayings. A short one goes home with you. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine.
